Slide 2 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Part V of the Indian constitution deals about union Executive.
  • Union Executive Consists of The President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister and Attorney General of India.
  • President is the head of the Indian states.

Slide 3 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 52 provides that there shall be a President of India and
  • Article 53 provides that the executive powers of the Union shall be vested in the President of India and shall be exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution.
  • the elected members of both Houses of Parliament; and

Slide 4 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The nominated members of the parliament & legislative assemblies and members of the legislative council cannot vote in the president election.
  • The electoral college consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the state Legislative Assemblies. [including National capital territory of Delhi and Puducherry]
  • Election to be held before the expiry of the tenure of the President in office (article 62 (1)). If the office falls vacant by death, resignation, removal or otherwise, election must be conducted within 6 months of the date of the vacancy. Once elected the President serves for 5 years.

Slide 5 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The President shall hold office for a term of five years
  • the President may, by writing under his hand addressed to the Vice-President, resign his office;
  • the President may, for violation of the Constitution, be removed from office by impeachment.

Slide 6 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • (b) Should be of not less than 35 years of age;
  • (c) Should be qualified for elections as a member of the House of people; [i.e he must be registered as a voter in an parliamentary constituency,]
  • (d) Should not hold any office of profit under the Government of India or any state Government or any local authority subject to the control of any of the said Government;

Slide 7 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The President is eligible to be re-elected without any restrictions.
  • But a person shall not be deemed to hold office of profit who is the president or the vice-president of the Union or the Governor of any state or the Minister of the Union or of any state.

Slide 8 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Condition of President’s Office: Article 59
  • If he is a member of either House of Parliament or a member of a House of the Legislature of any State, he shall be deemed to vacate his seat in that House on the date of entering into his office as President.
  • Official residence, emoluments, and allowances of President

Slide 9 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • He shall be also entitled to emoluments, allowances, and privileges determined by Parliament.
  • The emoluments and allowances of the President cannot be diminished or reduced during his term of office.
  • Apart from all these conditions and rules, the President of India is also entitled to certain allowances and privileges, as he is the first citizen of the country. The President of India is entitled to rent-free accommodation, allowances, and privileges by law.

Slide 10 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The salary of the President has undergone several changes since independence. Some of these changes were: In 1951, the President of India used to get a salary of Rs. 10,000 and 15000 rupees as an allowance.
  • In 1985, the President of India used to get a salary of Rs. 15,000 and 30000 rupees as an allowance.
  • Rashtrapati Bhavan is the President’s official residence, including reception halls, guest rooms, and offices. It is the largest residence of any head of state in the world.

Slide 11 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article – 60: Oath or affirmation by the President
  • According to Article 60, before entering upon his office, the president has to take an oath or an affirmation in the presence of the Chief Justice of India or, in his absence, the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court available, an oath or affirmation in the following form, that is to say—
  • ―I, A.B., do swear in the name of God that I will faithfully execute the office solemnly affirm of President (or discharge the functions of the President) of India and will to the best of my ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law and that I will devote myself to the service and wellbeing of the people of India.".

Slide 12 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • A resolution with the proposal to prefer such charges must be signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of the house and moved after giving at least 14 days advance notice. The resolution also needs to be passed by at least two-thirds majority of the house.
  • When the resolution is passed by one of the Houses, the other House must investigate the charges. The President has been granted the right to be present or to be represented in such investigations.
  • When the House investigating the charges passes the resolution by a two-thirds majority and declares the charges as sustaining, it results in removing the President from his office from the date of passing of the resolution

Slide 13 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 62 - Time of holding the election on expiry of the term and filling casual vacancies:
  • Article 62 provides for the filling up of the vacancy to the office of the President. It defines the terms of office of the person filling the casual vacancy as well as the time of holding elections to fill the vacancy.
  • An election to fill the vacancies, occurring due to the death, resignation or impeachment of the President, must be done as soon as possible. The elections, in any case, must be conducted within a time period of six months from the date of occurrence of the vacancy.

Slide 14 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The new person elected to the office of the President will be subject to all the provisions of Article 56 and will hold his office for a five-year term from the date of entering into the office.

Slide 15 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Privileges of the President: Article 361
  • As President, He will enjoy the degree of immunity. Under Article 361, the President is protected from being answerable to any court for:
  • The president shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him in the exercise of those powers and duties. However, the conduct of the president may be brought under review by any court, tribunal or body appointed or designed by either houses of parliament for the investigation of the charge in impeachment proceedings. Thus the immunity afforded to the president will not restrict the right of any person to bring suit against the government of India.

Slide 16 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • (a) a notice writing has been given to the president
  • (b) 2 months have passed after the service of such notice and
  • (c) the notice states the nature of proceeding, the cause of action, the name, residence and description of the party taking the proceedings and the relief claimed.

Slide 17 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 53 of the Indian Constitution states that all the executive powers of the Union will be vested in the President of India. President is allowed to exercise his executive powers through officers subordinate to him, directly or indirectly, in consonance to the provisions of the Constitution.
  • Appointment of the high authorities of the Constitution like the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers;
  • Right of being informed about all the national affairs;

Slide 18 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Appointment of the judges of the constitutional courts(Supreme Court and High Courts);
  • Appointment of the state Governors, the Attorney General, the Comptroller, and Auditor General, the Chief Commissioner and members of the Election Commission of India;
  • Administration of Union territories and appointment of the Chief Commissioners and Lieutenant Governor of the Centrally Administered Areas;

Slide 19 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 53 also states that the President shall be the Supreme Commander of all the Armed Forces of the Union of India. It also states that no specific provisions can reduce the scope of this general principle.
  • As the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of the Union, President has powers regarding:
  • Appointment of all the officers, including the appointment of the chiefs of the forces;

Slide 20 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The President forms the Indian diplomacy and helps the nation to maintain cordial relationships with countries across the globe.
  • All the Ambassadors and high commissioners in foreign nations are his representatives;
  • Prior to ratification by Parliament, the treaties and agreements with other nations, are negotiated by the President.

Slide 21 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • During the budget session, the President is the first to address the Parliament;
  • The President is empowered to summon a joint session in order to break the deadlock in the legislation process between the two Houses of the Parliament;
  • President sanction is mandatory in cases of provisions relating to:

Slide 22 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Legislative provisions relating to fundamental rights of the citizens of India require the President’s consent;
  • President’s consent is necessary for all the bills passed by the Parliament to become a law;
  • President is empowered to promulgate ordinances when the Parliament is not in session;

Slide 23 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • President receives reports of the Finance Commission and acts on its report.
  • The Contingency Funds of India are at the disposal of the President.
  • He exercises the power of grant of pardons and reprieves of punishments;

Slide 24 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 123 talks about the presidential powers to promulgate ordinances. An ordinance can be promulgated if:
  • The ordinance which is promulgated by the President will have the same effect as that of an act or law of the Parliament.
  • It shall be presented before both the Houses of Parliament for passing when it comes to the session;

Slide 25 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The ordinance may also expire if the resolutions disapproving it are passed by both the Houses of Parliament;
  • It can be withdrawn at any time by the President;
  • The ordinance must be in consonance to the Constitution of India else it shall be declared void.

Slide 26 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 72, provides for the provisions relating to the pardoning powers of the President. President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishments or remit suspend or commute the sentence given to a person by the court in the following cases:
  • When the sentence is granted through a court-martial;
  • When the sentence or punishment is given for offence of violation of any law relating to matters that fall in the ambit of Union’s executive powers;

Slide 27 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • A pardon completely absolves the offender from all sentences and punishments and disqualifications and places him in the same position as if he had never committed the offence.
  • Respite means awarding a lesser punishment on some special grounds e.g., the pregnancy of a woman offender.
  • Remission means reduction of the amount of sentence without changing its character, e.g. a sentence of one year may be remitted to 6 months.

  • President’s consent is necessary for all the bills passed by the Parliament to become a law;
  • President is empowered to promulgate ordinances when the Parliament is not in session;

Slide 23 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • President receives reports of the Finance Commission and acts on its report.
  • The Contingency Funds of India are at the disposal of the President.
  • He exercises the power of grant of pardons and reprieves of punishments;

Slide 24 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 123 talks about the presidential powers to promulgate ordinances. An ordinance can be promulgated if:
  • The ordinance which is promulgated by the President will have the same effect as that of an act or law of the Parliament.
  • It shall be presented before both the Houses of Parliament for passing when it comes to the session;

Slide 25 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The ordinance may also expire if the resolutions disapproving it are passed by both the Houses of Parliament;
  • It can be withdrawn at any time by the President;
  • The ordinance must be in consonance to the Constitution of India else it shall be declared void.

Slide 26 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 72, provides for the provisions relating to the pardoning powers of the President. President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishments or remit suspend or commute the sentence given to a person by the court in the following cases:
  • When the sentence is granted through a court-martial;
  • When the sentence or punishment is given for offence of violation of any law relating to matters that fall in the ambit of Union’s executive powers;

Slide 27 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • A pardon completely absolves the offender from all sentences and punishments and disqualifications and places him in the same position as if he had never committed the offence.
  • Respite means awarding a lesser punishment on some special grounds e.g., the pregnancy of a woman offender.
  • Remission means reduction of the amount of sentence without changing its character, e.g. a sentence of one year may be remitted to 6 months.

Slide 28 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Pardoning power of the President: Article 72
  • Commutation means exchange of one thing for another. It means substitution of one form of punishment for another of a lighter character, eg for rigorous imprisonment to simple imprisonment.

Slide 29 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 352 of the Constitution of India grants President, three kinds of emergency powers as well:
  • When a National Emergency is declared in case of external aggression or internal armed rebellion, the President holds the powers to declare a state of emergency. Thus the President’s rule gets established in the country. However, the prime minister and the Council of Ministers must recommend such an emergency;
  • When there exists a constitutional or law and order breakdown situation in a state, the President may declare a state of emergency in such cases. The state would then come under Governor’s rule;

Slide 30 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Emergency power of the President - 352
  • Whenever the financial stability of the nation or any country is seriously affected, the President has the right to intervene and direct the state to check and maintain public expenditure.

Slide 31 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • He acts as the President of India in case of death removal or resignation of the President of India.
  • Even if the President is unable to exercise his duties due to illness, absence or any other cause, the Vice-President can officiate any duties of the President.
  • During such tenures, the Vice-President is eligible to salaries, allowances that are payable to the President and ceases to be the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

  • The Parliament enacted the President (Discharge of Functions) Act 1969 by virtue of powers vested in the Parliament under article 70. In the absence of the President and the Vice- President the Chief Justice of India or the senior most Supreme court judge shall act as President till the new President takes office.
  • The Vice President (Article 63): Article 63 talks about the vice president of India.
  • There are some important functions and duties to be performed by the Vice-President of India. Article 64 and Article 65 of the Indian constitution talks about the following functions:

  • He protects the rights and privileges of the members of the Rajya Sabha;
  • The Vice-President shall perform the functions of President, in cases where the President is not able to perform his functions due to absence or illness etc until the President resumes his duty;

Slide 34 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The Vice-President shall act as President, If the vacancy is created for the post of President due to his resignation, removal, and death or otherwise until a new President is elected;
  • The period between the Vice-President acting as the President and the election of a new President can be extended for a maximum period of six months.

Slide 35 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • He should not be member of either house of the parliament
  • Should not hold any office of profit under Central Government, State Government, local or other authority. [Art.66(4)]

  • Removal – Resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by absolute Majority of total membership and agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority. Prior notice of 14 days to be served. No inquiry is required for removal of Vice-President.

Slide 38 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advice the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice:
  • Provided that the President may request the Council of Minsters to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
  • (2) The question whether, any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.

Slide 39 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • There should be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the president;
  • The Council of Ministers must have a Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President;
  • The President should exercise his functions and act in accordance with advice rendered by the Council of Ministers;

Slide 40 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The executive powers in India are exercised by the Council of Ministers. These ministers constitute ministries having cabinet minister, junior minister, etc. Before 2003, the size of ministries was not specified under any provision leading to a lot of chaos.
  • After the 91st amendment Act of 2003 came into existence, it marked a ceiling limit to the size of the ministries. The amendment stated that the strength of the Council of Ministers cannot exceed more than 15% of the total number of members of the Lok sabha or relevant Legislative Assembly of the state.
  • An exception was provided to the smaller states like Sikkim, Mizoram, and Goa, having a strength of lesser than 40 members in the legislative assemblies.

Slide 41 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Cabinets ministers: The cabinet ranks Minister are the head of their department. They attend the cabinet meeting as a matter of right however, a person can be appointed cabinet minister without a portfolio. The 44th constitution amendment act (1978) has confirmed constitution status on the cabinet minister.
  • Minister of state: The minister of state is formally of cabinet Status and are paid the same salary as the cabinet minister and they hold independent charge of their department but they attend the cabinet meeting only when invited.
  • Deputy ministers: The deputy ministers work under the minister of state and have no separate charge of a department. They get a lesser salary than the minister of state or cabinet minister. They assist the Minister in charge of a department or minister and take no part in cabinet.

Slide 42 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 102(2) and Article 191(2) provides for Anti-Defection laws regarding the members of Lok Sabha. According to this law, a member of a House, belonging to any political party, shall be disqualified as a member of the House on the following basis
  • If the person voluntarily gives up his/her membership of the political party to which he/she belongs; or
  • If the person votes or abstains from voting in contrary to any direction issued by the political party or by any person or authority authorized to give directions.

Slide 43 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Disqualification on defection on the ground of split in a political party
  • In either case, the prior permission of such political party, person or authority must be sought. The voting or abstention must be approved by the political party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of voting or abstention.
  • When a member of a House claims that he and any other members of his party have formed a group representing a faction emerging as a result of a split in his original political party. If such a group consists of one-third or more of the members of such a political party then the ministers cannot be disqualified under Anti-Defection laws.

Slide 44 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
  • (1A) The total number of Ministers including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed fifteen percent, of the total number of members of the House of the People.
  • (1B) A member of either House of Parliament belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of that House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified to be appointed as a Minister under clause (1) for duration of the period commencing from the date of his disqualification till the date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or where he contests any election to either House of Parliament before the expiry of such period, till the date on which he is declared elected whichever is earlier.

Slide 45 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • (4) Before a Minister enters upon his office, the President shall administer to him the oaths of office and of secrecy according to the forms set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.
  • (5) A Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of either House of Parliament shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister.
  • (6) The salaries and allowances of Ministers shall be such as Parliament may from time-to-time by law determine and, until Parliament so determines, shall be as specified in the Second Schedule.

Slide 46 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Article 75(3) Our Constitution clearly states that “The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to ‘House of the People”. It means that the Ministers are responsible to the Lok Sabha collectively.
  • The essence of collective responsibility is that, ‘the Minister must vote with the government, speak in defense of it if the Prime Minister insists, and he/she cannot afterwards reject criticism of his act, either in Parliament or in the constituencies, on the ground that he/she did not agree with the decision.’ This responsibility has two implications.
  • It means that every member of the Council of ministers accepts responsibility for each and every decision of the Cabinet. When a decision has been taken by the Cabinet, every Minister has to stand by it. If a Minister does not agree with the Cabinet decision, the only alternative left to him/her is to resign from the Council of Ministers.

Slide 47 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • 2. Also the vote of no-confidence against the Prime Minister is a vote against the whole Council of Ministers. Similarly, adverse vote in the Lok Sabha on any government bill or budget implies lack of confidence in the entire Council of Ministers, not only the mover of the bill.
  • Though the Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, they shall be individually responsible to the Head of the State i.e., President.
  • However, since the President has to act on the advice of the Prime Minister, in practice, this power is exercised by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister ask the Minister to resign.

Slide 48 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • In order to be a Minister, a person has to be a member of either of the two Houses of Parliament.

  • Within six months the Minister has to get himself/herself elected to either House of Parliament, failing which he/she ceases to be a Minister.

Slide 49 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • In our country, the Lok Sabha has a five-year term but it can be dissolved earlier. Article 83(2) of the Indian Constitution states that at the completion of five years term, from the starting date of Lok Sabha meetings, it can be dissolved.   • According to 85(b) The Lok Sabha can also be dissolved by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister before the expiry of its term.
  • The President can also dissolve the Lok Sabha, if he feels that a viable government cannot be formed, after the resignation or fall of a regime, as the case may be.

Slide 50 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The provision clearly states that any minister, who is not a member of either House of the Parliament, shall cease to be a minister after the period of six months from the date of his appointment.
  • The non-member must get elected to either House of the Parliament in order to continue as a Minister of Lok Sabha.

Slide 51 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • A convicted person cannot be appointed Chief Minister
  • When the question arose whether a convicted can be appointed as Chief Minister or not.
  • The issue was decided in the negative by the Supreme Court in the famous case known as Ms. J. Jayalalitha Case. It was held that any person who is convicted for a criminal offence and sentenced to imprisonment, for a period of two years, or more, cannot be appointed the Chief Minister of any State under Article 164(1) of the Indian Constitution.

Slide 52 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Governor: constitutional - union government nominates Governor in each state.

  • must be a citizen of India; and

Slide 54 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The Governor must not be a member of either House of Parliament and House of the Legislature of any State.

Slide 55 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Subject to the foregoing provisions of this Article, a Governor shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office.

Study notes · Source slide deck: constitution

Slide 1 · [Image text, OCR]

  • Constitutional Law, cyber law, ip law and professional ethics

Slide 2 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Among the noble aims and objectives of the constitution, the founding fathers accorded the highest place to ‘justice’. The preamble speaks of “we the people of India” resolving to secure “Justice- social, economic & political” to “all its citizens”.
  • The juxta position of words and concepts in the preamble is important “Justice’ is placed higher than the other principles of ‘Liberty’, Equality and Fraternity. Again, the preamble clearly enjoins precedence to social and economic justice over political justice.
  • The constitution lays down the structure, appointment, transfer and removal of judges and denies, delimits and demarcates the role and functions of every organ of the state including the judiciary. By all these, independence of judiciary is established.

Slide 3 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • The Union Judiciary (Articles 124-147): Supreme Court stands at the Apex
  • Establishment and Constitution of Supreme Court: There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges (now increased to 30)
  • Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the States as the President may deem necessary for the purpose and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty- five years

Slide 4 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Hold office – Till the age of sixty-five years:
  • has been for at least five years a Judge of a High Court or of two or more such Courts in succession
  • has been for at least ten years an advocate of a High Court or of two or more such courts in succession

Slide 5 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Apart from the above mentioned qualifications expressly prescribed by the Constitution, the implied qualifications required are: unimpeachable character and integrity; impartiality, independence; equanimity; incorruptibility.
  • As stated under Art.124 (2), a judge of the Supreme court shall hold an office until he attains the age of sixty-five years. He may resign before the age of retirement by addressing his letter of resignation to the president.

Slide 6 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • Supported by a majority two-thirds of the members of the House present and voting
  • V. Ramaswami J was the first judge against whom impeachment proceedings were initiated. In 1993, the motion was brought up in Lok Sabha but failed to secure the required two-thirds majority.
  • Soumitra Sen J of the Calcutta High Court resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha passed an impeachment motion against him. He was the first judge to have been impeached by the Upper House for misconduct.

Slide 7 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • In 2015, 58 members of the Rajya Sabha moved an impeachment notice against J.B. Pardiwala J of the Gujarat High Court for his “objectionable remarks on the issue of reservation.”

  • In March 2018, opposition parties signed a draft proposal for moving an impeachment motion against Dipak Misra CJI.

  • If at any time it appears to the President that a question of law or fact has arisen, or is likely to arise, which is of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the opinion of the Supreme Court upon it, he may refer the question to that Court for consideration and the Court may, after such hearing as it thinks fit, report to the President its opinion thereon.
  • Such advisory opinion of the Supreme Court may be rendered at the instance of the president of India which may enable parliament to pass appropriate legislation or to introspect and effect suitable amendments to the existing law.

Slide 15 · State Judiciary

  • Normally there is one High Court in every State but there can be only one High Court for two or more States as well according to the constitution.

Slide 32 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

Slide 24 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352 to 360)

  • A novel feature of the Indian Constitution is the way in which the normal peace-time federalism, can be adopted to an emergency situation. The framers of the Constitution felt that, in an emergency, the Centre should have overriding powers to control and direct all aspects of administration and legislation throughout the country.
  • The Indian Constitution envisages three types of emergencies
  • Emergency arising from a threat to security of India or any part of its territory;

Slide 25 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352 to 360)

  • It occurs whenever there is imbalance within the Country, whether wholly or partly.
  • Ultimate aim of government is to secure good life & safe life to its citizen .
  • If we analyse the ex 1, 2 & 3"emergency in all the cases. The social equilibrium of the country was imbalanced and security of the citizen was on the threat.

Slide 26 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352 to 360)

  • National Emergency (352): If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or any part of its territory is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion, he may proclaim a state of emergency under Article 352.
  • If not, it shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament. If Parliament does not approve of it within one month, it will become invalid.
  • So far, there have been three occasions when emergency of the first category was proclaimed by the President: 1962 (Chinese aggression), 1971 (Indo-Pakistan war before the formation of Bangladesh) and 1975 (internal emergency).

Slide 27 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352 to 360)

  • State Emergency (356): If the President is satisfied on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise that a situation has arisen in which the Government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, he can proclaim an emergency under Article 356 and 365.
  • He may assume to himself all or any of the functions of the State or he may vest all or any of those functions in the Governor or any other executive authority; or
  • he may make any other incidental or consequential provisions necessary to give effect to the objects of the Proclamation

Slide 28 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352 to 360)

  • The proclamation may be revoked subsequently; if not, it shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament, if Parliament does not approve of it within two months, it will become ineffective.
  • During the period of emergency, - the State is empowered to suspend the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 19 of the Indian Constitution.

Slide 29 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352 to 360)

  • Financial Emergency (ARTICLE 360): If the President is satisfied that a situation has arisen whereby the financial stability or credit of India or any part of it is threatened, he may declare a financial emergency under Article 360. The proclamation in this case also should be approved by Parliament as in the other two cases of emergency.
  • When such a proclamation is in operation, the centre can give directions to any State to observe such canons of financial propriety as may be specified in the directions. It may also give such other directions as the President may deem necessary and adequate for the purpose. Any such directions may provide for the reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in the State.

Slide 30 · EMERGENCY (ARTICLE 352)

  • The 44th Amendment makes article 360 self-contained. It provides that the proclamation of financial emergency will cease to be in operation at the expiry of two months unless it has been approved by both Houses of Parliament. Such a proclamation may be revoked or varied by the President by a subsequent proclamation. But if the Lok Sabha is dissolved during the period of two months and resolution is approved by the Rajya Sabha, but not by the Lok Sabha the proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiry of 30 days from the date on which the new Lok Sabha sits unless before the expiry of 30 days a resolution approving proclamation is passed by the Lok Sabha.
  • The duration of a proclamation of financial emergency will be in operation for two months and unless approved by President it shall cease to operate at the expiry of two months' period.

Slide 31 · Constitutional Law, Cyber Law and Professional Ethics

  • AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION OF INDIA

Slide 32 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • The Indian Constitution came into force on 26th January 1950. The provisions of the constitution were so designed to meet the social, economic conditions prevailing at that time. To meet the changing conditions, there shall be an appropriate mechanism to alter the provisions of the constitution. Such mechanism is called the “Amendment of the Constitution”.
  • Amendment of the Constitution is done under Article 368
  • An amendment to the Constitution of India may be allowed by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of the Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha). The bill has to be passed in each house by a majority, which is more than 50% of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the House present and voting.

Slide 33 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • After acquiring the majority, the Bill is presented to the President who will then give his assent to the Bill.
  • In the case of amendment of provisions mentioned in Article 368, It needs to be ratified by not less than half of the states. Ratification should be done by a resolution passed by the state legislature.
  • Basic Structure: The Basic Structure Doctrine states there are certain fundamental structures and founding principles of the constitution which make the backbone of the constitution. In simple terms, they are ideologies of the constitution which are essential for the survival of the constitution

Slide 34 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • Shankari Prasad v. Union of India ( AIR 1951 SC 455) was the first time when the question of whether Fundamental Rights enshrined under Part III of the Constitution of India, can be amended under Article 368. The Five Judge Bench had stated, Article 368 provides for general and strict power to the Parliament of India to amend the Constitution.

Slide 35 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967 AIR 1643) was the case where three amendments, namely, the first, fourth, and seventeenth amendments, were challenged. The bench had eleven judges out of which the majority six-judge bench held that Part 3 of the Constitution (Fundamental Rights) could not be amended by the Parliament of India.
  • Keshvananda Bharati v. Union of India (1973) 4 SCC 225) was a landmark case where for the first time, the Supreme Court brought in the doctrine of Basic Structure. The court overruled the judgment of the Golaknath case, The apex court held that article 368 of the Constitution does not empower the Parliament to change, damage, or alter the basic structure of the Constitution of India. The Preamble is actually the basic structure of the Constitution of India.

Slide 36 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • 42nd Amendment to the Constitution of India added the words “secular” and “socialist” to the Constitution of India and added clause 4 and 5 to Article 368. This amendment recognized the ultimate power of the Parliament in amending the Constitution of India even after the Supreme Court judgments of Keshvananda Bharati and Raj Narayan.

Slide 37 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • Recent trends in India's constitutional development show the basic structure doctrine is increasingly important for protecting core constitutional principles from amendment.
  • The Supreme Court, establishing this doctrine in the Kesavanada Bharati (1973), acts to safeguard foundational aspects like Constitutional Supremacy, rule of law, judicial review and Secularism though the exact boundaries remain subject to judicial interpretation and debate. This ongoing evolution highlights the tension between adapting to societal changes and preserving the Indian Constitution’s enduring integrity.

Slide 38 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • The doctrine acts as a legal shield, preventing Parliament from altering the Constitution's fundamental features.
  • The Supreme Court can review and strike down constitutional amendments that violate the Constitution's basic structure.
  • Commonly accepted elements of the basic structure include constitutional supremacy, rule of law, judicial review, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, and the protection of fundamental rights.

Slide 39 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • The doctrine continues to be applied by the Supreme Court, with judgments often debating the scope of what constitutes the "basic structure".
  • There is an ongoing need for the Constitution to adapt to changing societal needs while maintaining its core values and principles.
  • While the doctrine is widely accepted, its applicability to ordinary legislation (not just amendments) and the precise definition of its components are subjects of ongoing legal discussion.

Slide 40 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • The basic structure doctrine serves to protect the democratic foundations of the Indian Constitution from potential abuse of power.
  • By preserving the Constitution's fundamental integrity, the doctrine contributes to the stability of the Indian legal and political landscape.
  • The doctrine has profoundly influenced Indian constitutional law, acting as a "most potent tool" for maintaining checks and balances within the democratic system

Slide 41 · Abrogation of Article 370

  • Article 370 gave special status to Jammu & Kashmir.
  • After repealing Article 370, he entire Indian Constitution extended to Jammu and Kashmir.
  • The Supreme Court (2023 judgment) upheld the abrogation, stating that federalism in India is asymmetric and Parliament acted within its powers.

Slide 32 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • The Indian Constitution came into force on 26th January 1950. The provisions of the constitution were so designed to meet the social, economic conditions prevailing at that time.   • Amendment of the Constitution is done under Article 368
  • An amendment to the Constitution of India may be allowed by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of the Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha). The bill has to be passed in each house by a majority, which is more than 50% of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the House present and voting.

  • After acquiring the majority, the Bill is presented to the President who will then give his assent to the Bill.
  • In the case of amendment of provisions mentioned in Article 368, It needs to be ratified by not less than half of the states. Ratification should be done by a resolution passed by the state legislature.
  • Basic Structure: The Basic Structure Doctrine states there are certain fundamental structures and founding principles of the constitution which make the backbone of the constitution. In simple terms, they are ideologies of the constitution which are essential for the survival of the constitution

Slide 34 · AMENDMENT OF CONSTITUTION

  • Shankari Prasad v. Union of India ( AIR 1951 SC 455) was the first time when the question of whether Fundamental Rights enshrined under Part III of the Constitution of India, can be amended under Article 368.   • Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967 AIR 1643) was the case where three amendments, namely, the first, fourth, and seventeenth amendments, were challenged.   • Keshvananda Bharati v. Union of India (1973) 4 SCC 225) was a landmark case where for the first time, the Supreme Court brought in the doctrine of Basic Structure. The court overruled the judgment of the Golaknath case, The apex court held that article 368 of the Constitution does not empower the Parliament to change, damage, or alter the basic structure of the Constitution of India.   • 42nd Amendment to the Constitution of India added the words “secular” and “socialist” to the Constitution of India and added clause 4 and 5 to Article 368. Slide 37 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • Recent trends in India's constitutional development show the basic structure doctrine is increasingly important for protecting core constitutional principles from amendment.
  • The Supreme Court, establishing this doctrine in the Kesavanada Bharati (1973), acts to safeguard foundational aspects like Constitutional Supremacy, rule of law, judicial review and Secularism though the exact boundaries remain subject to judicial interpretation and debate. This ongoing evolution highlights the tension between adapting to societal changes and preserving the Indian Constitution’s enduring integrity.

Slide 38 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • The doctrine acts as a legal shield, preventing Parliament from altering the Constitution's fundamental features.
  • The Supreme Court can review and strike down constitutional amendments that violate the Constitution's basic structure.
  • Commonly accepted elements of the basic structure include constitutional supremacy, rule of law, judicial review, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, and the protection of fundamental rights.

Slide 39 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • The doctrine continues to be applied by the Supreme Court, with judgments often debating the scope of what constitutes the "basic structure".
  • There is an ongoing need for the Constitution to adapt to changing societal needs while maintaining its core values and principles.
  • While the doctrine is widely accepted, its applicability to ordinary legislation (not just amendments) and the precise definition of its components are subjects of ongoing legal discussion.

Slide 40 · Recent Trends and Constitutional Development

  • By preserving the Constitution's fundamental integrity, the doctrine contributes to the stability of the Indian legal and political landscape.
  • The doctrine has profoundly influenced Indian constitutional law, acting as a "most potent tool" for maintaining checks and balances within the democratic system

  • After repealing Article 370, he entire Indian Constitution extended to Jammu and Kashmir.
  • The Supreme Court (2023 judgment) upheld the abrogation, stating that federalism in India is asymmetric and Parliament acted within its powers.

Professional code of ethics may be referred. b) Collection of all information, data, and facts relevant to the situation. c)Rank the moral options i.e., priority in application through value system. d) Not discuss with colleagues and obtain their perspectives, priorities, and suggestions on various alternatives. notes.text:
Computational problem solving is a process, not just coding. Begin by understanding the goal and constraints, then represent the problem, choose a method, implement it in Python, and test the result against cases that matter.

Keep the problem statement separate from the program. A computer follows exact instructions; it does not infer missing requirements. Use examples to clarify input, output, and edge cases before writing code.

Python can be used interactively to explore an expression or in a saved .py file for a repeatable program. The course connects algorithmic reasoning to syntax, data, control flow, and testing; each later topic supplies a tool in that larger process.

notes.text:
Model the river puzzle as a state-space search. The farmer, wolf, goat, and cabbage begin on one bank. The boat carries the farmer plus at most one passenger. A state records which bank each item occupies.

A state is unsafe if the farmer leaves the wolf alone with the goat, or the goat alone with the cabbage. A legal move changes the farmer's bank and optionally moves one item with him; reject any move that creates an unsafe state.

Search the remaining legal states until the goal is reached, and keep a record of visited states to avoid cycling. The key computational idea is to make constraints explicit, generate only valid successors, and verify that the final state satisfies the goal.

notes.text:
Separate the stages of solving a computational problem. Analysis identifies the required result, inputs, constraints, and special cases. Design turns that understanding into an algorithm or data representation. Implementation expresses the design in a programming language.

Testing compares actual outputs with expected behavior on representative and boundary inputs. A syntax error means the program violates Python's grammar; a logic error means it runs but computes the wrong result. Passing one example is not proof of correctness, so use cases that challenge assumptions.

There may be several valid designs. Compare them against clarity, correctness, and resource requirements instead of treating the first working program as the only solution.

notes.text:
Hardware is the physical machine; software is the instructions and data it uses. A computer accepts input, stores and processes data, and produces output. The processor executes instructions, memory holds active data and programs, and input/output devices connect the computer to its environment.

Operating-system software manages hardware resources and provides services to applications. Application software performs tasks for a user. A program is not the hardware itself: it is a representation of operations that the machine executes.

Distinguish primary memory, which the processor can access directly while programs run, from persistent secondary storage. The distinction helps explain where instructions and data reside at each stage of computation.

notes.text:
A digital computer processes encoded data through coordinated components. The input unit supplies data and instructions; memory stores them; the processor fetches and executes instructions; and output devices present results. The arithmetic and logic unit performs calculations and comparisons, while the control unit coordinates instruction execution.

Registers and main memory are fast working storage but are volatile: their contents normally disappear when power is removed. Secondary storage such as an SSD retains files. The processor does not directly understand a human problem; software encodes the steps and data in forms the machine can process.

When tracing a program, follow both the changing values in memory and the sequence of instructions executed by the processor.

notes.text:
A Python program is built from statements and expressions arranged with meaningful indentation. A statement performs an action, such as assigning a value or calling a function; an expression produces a value. Names identify variables and functions, while literals provide fixed values.

Indentation is part of Python's syntax: statements at the same indentation level belong to the same block, and a block follows a header ending in a colon. Comments explain intent to a human reader but are ignored by Python.

Keep a program readable by using descriptive names, consistent indentation, and small sections that each have a clear purpose. Read errors from the first reported line, then check nearby syntax and block boundaries.

notes.text:
print() writes a readable representation of values to standard output. It can display one value or several values separated by commas. The sep argument controls the text between values, and end controls what is written after them; by default, values are separated by a space and the call ends with a newline.

Strings need quotation marks in source code, but print() displays their contents without those delimiters. Printing is useful for user-facing output and for tracing a program while debugging.

Remember that printing a value is different from returning it from a function. Output is text sent to the terminal; a returned value can be used by later expressions.

notes.text:
A variable name refers to a value used by a program. Assignment evaluates the right-hand expression and binds the resulting value to the name on the left. Later assignment can bind that same name to another value.

Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the object, and a name can refer to objects of different types at different points in a program. Choose names that describe their role, and do not confuse the name with the storage location or with the value itself.

When tracing code, update a name's binding after each assignment. This simple state trace exposes errors caused by using an old or unexpected value.

notes.text:
Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not copy an object's identity into the name. The built-in id(x) returns an integer that is unique and constant for that object's lifetime. In CPython it often corresponds to a memory address, but Python code should not rely on that implementation detail.

Use == to compare values for equality. Use is only when object identity is what matters, most commonly to test a singleton such as None. Two separate objects can compare equal while having different identities.

For mutable objects, two names may refer to the same object; changing it through either name is visible through both. This is why identity and value equality must be kept distinct.

notes.text:
input() reads a line of text and returns it as a string. A prompt can be supplied to tell the user what to enter, but the returned value is still text. Convert it before arithmetic: use int() for an integer or float() for a decimal quantity, and handle invalid input when the program requires robustness.

Separate reading, conversion, validation, and computation. This makes it clear whether a failure came from unexpected text, an out-of-range value, or the algorithm itself.

Do not assume that typing digits makes the result numeric: input() returns a string until the program explicitly converts it.

notes.text:
Operators combine operands to compute or test values. Arithmetic operators perform numeric operations; relational operators such as <, ==, and >= compare values and produce a Boolean result; membership operators in and not in test whether a value occurs in a collection or string.

Keep the result type in mind: 5 > 2 is a Boolean, while 5 + 2 is numeric. Division with / produces a floating-point result in Python, even when both inputs are integers; // is floor division.

Use parentheses to make mixed expressions easy to read, and test boundary cases for comparisons.

notes.text:
Bitwise operators act on the binary representation of integers. AND keeps a bit only when both corresponding bits are 1; OR keeps it when either is 1; XOR keeps it when the bits differ; complement inverts the representation under Python's integer model. Left and right shifts move bit positions and correspond to multiplication or floor division by powers of two for nonnegative integers.

Bitwise operations are useful for masks, flags, and low-level encodings. They are different from Boolean and, or, and not, which work with truth values and short-circuit evaluation.

Write small binary examples before combining masks; the bit-by-bit view is the safest way to check a result.

notes.text:
Boolean logic combines conditions. not negates truth, and is true only when both operands are truthy, and or is true when at least one is truthy. Python evaluates and and or from left to right and may stop as soon as the result is determined.

With A and B, Python skips B if A is false. With A or B, it skips B if A is true. This short-circuit rule supports safe guards such as checking that a value is not None before using it.

These operators return one of their operands, not necessarily a Boolean. Use explicit comparisons when the code's intent would otherwise be unclear.

defs.text: A syntactically valid combination of values, names, and operators that Python evaluates to a value.
A value or expression on which an operator acts.
The priority that determines which operator binds first in an expression.
The grouping direction used when operators of equal precedence occur together.

notes.text:
Expressions evaluate to values. A literal such as 123, 3.5, or a string is already an expression. A variable name is also an expression because evaluating the name retrieves its current value. Operators combine operands to build larger expressions.

Operators and operands. A unary operator acts on one operand, a binary operator on two, and Python's conditional expression has three parts: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. Parentheses explicitly group a subexpression.

Precedence chooses which operation binds first. In 2 + 3 * 4, multiplication has higher precedence, so Python evaluates 3 * 4 first and returns 14. Parentheses can override the default grouping; use them when the intended order should be obvious to a reader.

Associativity breaks ties. Operators at the same precedence level follow their associativity rule. Subtraction groups left to right, so 10 - 3 - 2 means (10 - 3) - 2 = 5. Exponentiation groups right to left, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512. Do not assume every operator groups in the same direction.

Where the result appears. The interactive interpreter echoes the value of a bare expression. A saved .py program needs print(expression) when the result should appear in the terminal.

rapid.q: What is the difference between precedence and associativity?
rapid.a: Precedence ranks different operators; associativity chooses grouping among operators at the same precedence.

rapid.q: Why does a script use print() for a result?
rapid.a: A script does not echo a bare expression the way the interactive interpreter does; print() writes the value to the terminal.

notes.text:
Sequential control runs statements in order; selection chooses a branch. Python executes a block from top to bottom unless a control statement changes the path. An if/elif/else chain evaluates conditions in order and executes the first matching branch.

Write conditions that cover the intended cases without overlap where possible. Put the most specific conditions before broader ones, and include an else branch when every remaining case needs a defined response.

Iteration repeats a block while progressing toward a stopping condition. A for loop visits items from an iterable; a while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. For each loop, identify initialization, the repeated work, the state update, and the exit condition.

A for loop is often the clearest choice when processing a known collection or range. A while loop is useful when the number of repetitions depends on a changing condition. Make sure every path through a while-loop body moves toward termination.

break exits the nearest loop and continue skips to its next iteration. Use them sparingly so the loop's flow remains easy to trace.

notes.text:
A Python string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Indexing selects one character, slicing selects a half-open range, and concatenation combines strings. A slice s[a:b] includes index a and stops before index b.

Common methods return new strings: lower() changes letter case, strip() removes edge whitespace, and split() separates text into a list. Because strings are immutable, a method does not modify the original string in place.

Check index boundaries and empty strings when processing input. For readable output that mixes text and values, use formatted string literals rather than manual concatenation.

Slide 1 · PROBLEM SOLVING

  • Department of Computer Science and Engineering

Slide 2 · A list is a collection that allows us to put many things / values under a single

  • Values in the list are called elements / items.
  • List is an ordered sequence of items.
  • List is a linear data structure where elements have linear ordering.

Slide 3 · List Characteristics

  • Elements in the list can be heterogeneous (different datatypes) or homogeneous
  • Elements are accessed using indexing operation (also called subscript notation).
  • List index always starts >>> print (numbers[1])

Slide 4 · List Characteristics

  • List is iterable - is eager and not lazy.
  • AssignmentAssignment ofof oneone listlist toto anotheranother causescauses bothboth toto referrefer toto thethe samesame listlist.
  • List can be sliced. This creates a new (sub)list.

Slide 5 · List Characteristics

  • Lists are mutable, as list can grow or shrink .
  • o We can change an element of a list.
  • >>> numbers[0]=10 # index operation is used.

Slide 6 · List Characteristics

  • List is iterable - is eager and not lazy.
  • Ex: (ii) number=[10,20,30,40,50] Ex: (i) numbers=[55,88,45,12]
  • List can be nested. We can have list of lists.

Slide 7 · List Characteristics

  • Assignment of one list to another causes both to refer to the same list.
  • Ex: >>> list1=[12,44,55,89,11,24]
  • Note: In Python, the id() function is a built-in function that returns the unique identifier of an object.

Slide 8 · List Characteristics

  • List can be sliced. This creates a new (sub)list.
  • Given lst1 = [12,44,55,89,11,24]
  • >>> llst22 = llst1[::]1[ ] ## creates a copy off llst1.1 NNot same as llst22 = llst11

Slide 9 · Ex: >>> lst = [9, 41, 12, 3, 74, 15] >>> lst1=[10,20,[30,40,50]]

  • >>> lst[1:3] >>> lst1[2][1]
  • [9, 41, 12, 3, 74, 15]

Slide 10 · Creation of Lists

  • List items are surrounded by square brackets and the elements in the list are
  • A list element can be any Python object - even another list.
  • politicians=['modi', 'jayalalitha', 'yediyurappa','devegowda',['parikar', 'swaraj',

Slide 11 · Built In Functions

  • There are a number of functions built into Python that take lists
  • >>> numsnums = [3,[3, 41,41, 12,12, 9,9, 74,74, 15]15]

Slide 12 · List Operations

  • We can create a new list by adding two existing lists together.
  • >>> list1 = [10,20,30,40,50]
  • [10,20,30,40,50, 100,200,300,400,500]

Slide 13 · List Operations

  • Allows for the multiplying of the list n times
  • >>> list1 = [10,20,30,40,50]
  • [10,20,30,40,50,10,20,30,40,50]

Slide 14 · List Operations

  • Used to arrange the elements of a list.
  • EEx: >>>>>> lilist1t1 = [10[10, 11, -2,2 22, 9]9]
  • [-2, 1, 2, 9, 10]

Slide 15 · List Operations

  • allows to add element at the end of list.
  • >>> list1 = [10,20,30,40,50]
  • [10,20,30,40,50,22]

Slide 16 · List Operations

  • Allows to add an element at particular position in the list.
  • >>> list1 = [10,20,30,40,50]
  • [10,20,30,55,40,50]

Slide 17 · List Operations

  • adds the specified list elements (or any iterable) to the
  • >>>list1.extend([11,22,33,44,55])
  • [10,20,30,40,50,11,22,33,44,55]

Slide 18 · pop() & remove()

  • allows to remove element from a list by using pop() or remove() functions.
  • One uses index value (pop),another uses value(remove) as reference to remove
  • >>>list1.pop(2) # using pop() >>> list1.remove(40) #using remove()

Slide 19 · List Operations

  • returns number of occurrences of value.
  • >>> list1 = [10,20,30,40,50]

Slide 20 · List Operations

  • return first index of a value. Raises ValueError if
  • the value is not present.
  • >>> list1 = [10,20,30,40,50]

Slide 21 · List Operators

  • in returns True if a particular item exists in the list. otherwise False
  • not in operator returns True if the element is not present, otherwise False
  • Ex: >>> list1 = [10,2.2,(22,33,43),('python') ] # heterogeneous list.

Slide 22 · We may at times need to compare data items in the two lists to perform certain operations

  • >>> list1 = [10,2.2,(22,33,43]

Slide 23 · List Traversal

  • Image-only source page; see the visual page locator in datasets/content-index.json.

Slide 24 · 1. List using For Loop:

  •  The for loop in Python is used to iterate over a sequence (list, tuple, string) or other
  •  Loop continues until we reach the last item in the sequence
  •  The body of for loop is separated from the rest of the code using indentation.

Slide 25 · Slide page 25

  • Image-only source page; see the visual page locator in datasets/content-index.json.

Slide 26 · 2. List using while loop:

  • The while loop in Python is used to iterate over a block of code as long as the test expression
  • When the condition is tested and the result is false, the loop body will be skipped and the
  • first statement after the while loop will be executed.

Slide 1 · Python Modules and PIP

  • Department of Computer Science and Engineering
  • Prof. Kundhavai K R, CSE Department

Slide 2 · Introduction to Modules

  • Python provides many built-in modules like math, os, random,
  • You can also create your own modules by saving functions in a
  • You can also include the third-party modules in the python code.

Slide 3 · Advantages of Modules

  • Reusability: Write code once and reuse it across multiple programs, reducing duplication and saving development time.
  • Modularity: Break large programs into smaller, logical parts, making code easier to develop, debug, and maintain.
  • Separate Namespace: Each module has its own namespace, preventing naming conflicts between functions or variables in different modules.

Slide 4 · Types of Modules

  • User-Defined Modules (Creating your own modules).

Slide 5 · What is PIP?

  • PIP = Pip Installs Packages Tool to install/manage third-party python packages.
  • pip install package_name pip uninstall package_name pip list

Slide 6 · Types of Modules

  • Provided by Python by default (e.g., math, os, random, datetime) No installation needed Useful for common programming tasks

Slide 7 · Types of Modules

  • Ways to import Built-in Modules

Slide 8 · Types of Modules

  • Modules created by the programmer Stored as .py files containing functions, classes, or variables Used to organize and reuse your own code

Slide 9 · Types of Modules

  • my_utils.py → your helper functions calculator.py → custom math operations string_ops.py → string-related utilities

Slide 10 · Types of Modules

  • Developed by the Python community
  • Must be installed using PIP (e.g., numpy, scikit-learn, pillow)
  • Extend Python with advanced or specialized features

Slide 11 · Types of Modules

  • Third-Party Modules (via PIP)
  • numpy → numerical computing pandas → data analysis matplotlib → plotting & visualization requests → working with APIs Pillow → image processing

Slide 1 · Solving- UE26CS151A

Slide 2 · Why Do We Need Python Environments?

  • Different projects may require different Python or package
  • Virtual environments isolate project dependencies from one
  • system Python and simplifies deployment

Slide 3 · Introduction to Python Environments

  • A Python environment is a workspace where Python and its
  • Separate environments help avoid conflicts between package
  • Key topics covered: virtual environments, venv, pip and

Slide 4 · What is a Virtual Environment?

  • Python provides the built-in venv module for creating virtual
  • No extra installation needed — venv ships with Python 3.3 and later
  • Each environment behaves like its own self-contained Python installation

Slide 5 · Creating a Virtual Environment

  • Navigate to the project directory first
  • Create an environment using venv:
  • Environment names such as myenv, venv or .venv are common

Slide 6 · Activating a Virtual Environment

  • An active environment is shown by (myenv) in the terminal prompt

Slide 7 · Deactivating a Virtual Environment

  • Use deactivate when finished working with the environment
  • Deactivation does not delete the environment — it simply exits it
  • The same environment can be reactivated anytime later

Slide 8 · What is pip?

  • pip is Python’s package installer
  • python -m pip install numpy
  • Works both inside a virtual environment and with the system

Slide 9 · Installing Packages

  • Install one package or several packages together
  • Packages can be imported into Python right after installation
  • python -m pip install numpy==1.26.4

Slide 10 · Upgrading, Uninstalling & Viewing Packages

  • python -m pip install --upgrade numpy
  • python -m pip uninstall numpy
  • Package details and dependency list:

Slide 11 · requirements.txt

  • python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
  • python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Typical project layout: program.py, requirements.txt,

Slide 12 · Sharing a Python Project

  • Share the project folder along with requirements.txt — not the
  • Another user creates a fresh virtual environment on their own
  • They install every dependency from requirements.txt in one

Slide 13 · Complete Workflow & Example: NumPy Project

  • Create project → create venv → activate → install packages →
  • Example: setting up a NumPy project
  • python -m pip install numpy

Slide 14 · Why Use python -m pip?

  • Runs pip using the specifically selected Python interpreter
  • Reduces confusion when multiple Python installations or
  • python -m pip install package_name

Slide 15 · Virtual Environment vs System Python

  • System Python: packages are shared across many projects, so
  • Virtual environment: packages are isolated per project,
  • Changes to system Python can affect the whole machine; venv

Slide 16 · Quick Reference – Important Commands

  • python -m pip install numpy | python -m pip
  • python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt |
  • python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Slide 17 · Key Takeaways

  • Virtual environment = isolated workspace for a Python project
  • pip = tool used to install and manage Python packages
  • Using virtual environments makes Python development cleaner,

Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we will start with a new module on electrochemical equilibrium.

Key details

  • In this module we are going to study about electrode potential and cell potential.
  • We will derive the Nernst equation.
  • Then we discuss the different types of electrodes.
  • We will look at reference electrodes and also talk about concentration cells.
  • And finally, we will discuss about ion selective electrodes.
  • In today's class we will discuss the origin of electrode potential, we will talk about cell potential and we will derive Nernst equation.
  • Electrochemical equilibria deals with electrochemistry, which is a branch of chemistry which deals with the interconversion of chemical energy and electrical energy.
  • In the galvanic cell, we have chemical energy getting converted into electrical energy.
  • It is the energy in a chemical reaction.
  • Now the reaction has to be a spontaneous reaction because we are not going to provide any energy from outside.
  • The chemical energy has to produce electrical energy.
  • And since we are going to produce electrical energy, that is power, there has to be exchange of electrons.
  • Therefore, we have to have detox reaction.
  • Examples of galvanic cell would be in batteries and fuel cells.
  • We convert electrical energy to chemical energy.
  • Electrical energy is provided externally and.
  • We want to get chemical energy, meaning we want to make a chemical reaction happen.
  • We require a non-spontaneous redox reaction in an electrolytic cell.
  • We use such cells in electroplating, electro refining, and many other metallurgical processes.
  • Whenever we do electrochemical studies, the first thing we require is a redox reaction because we are talking of conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy or electrical energy into chemical energy, and both require an exchange of electrons.
  • And one thing we should always remember that oxidation and reduction have to happen simultaneously.
  • The second requirement is that of electrodes.
  • These oxidation and reduction reactions have to happen at the anode and cathode respectively.
  • And the third requirement would be electrolytic conductance.
  • The conductance is through the movement of ions.
  • We have to remember that electrons cannot move through the electrolyte.
  • It's only the ions which are going to cause electrolytic conductance.
  • We can also have molten electrolytes.

Study notes · Source slide deck: Experiential learning Based on corrosion chemistry

The slide deck is rewritten here as searchable lesson notes. Each subsection states the slide heading and its concise teaching points; page citations lead back to the indexed source image when visual details are needed.

Slide 1 · ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY (UE26CY151 A,B)

  • Department of Science and Humanities

Slide 2 · ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

  • The rate of a chemical reaction, in general, increases with rise in temperature
  • Increase in conductance of the medium- ions migrate fast at higher temperature.
  • However, if corrosion is due to dissolved gases like O2, CO2, etc., the rate of corrosion decreases with increase in temperature as the solubility of these gases in the medium decreases

Slide 3 · ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

  • In general, lower the pH of the corrosion medium, higher is the
  • At low pH ,concentration of H+ ions is high; H+ ions help for cathodic reaction facilitating anodic oxidation of the metal
  • However, some metals like Al undergo fast corrosion in

Slide 4 · ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

  • As the conductivity of the corrosion medium increases, the corrosion rate also increases
  • Higher the conductivity of the medium, faster the ions can migrate between the anodic and cathodic regions of the corrosion cell
  • Faster will be the exchange of electrons at the electrode surfaces; corrosion rate increases

Slide 5 · ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY

  • Experiential Learning – UNIT 2 (supplementary material)
  • Corrosion rate increases with increase in the humidity in the medium.
  • The presence of moisture in the atmosphere provides the conducting medium for the formation of galvanic cell, facilitating corrosion of the metal.
