notes.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we'll start with unit 3, so that is module 5, and we are going to learn about energy storage devices.

Key details

  • Then we learn about modern batteries like zinc air battery, lithium batteries, and specifically lithium ion battery.
  • Then we study about reserve batteries and then fuel cells.
  • principle working and efficiency of fuel cells.
  • We also look at three different types of fuel cells.
  • Hydrogen oxygen alkaline fuel cells carbon monoxide oxygen solid oxide fuel cell and methanol oxygen polynomial membrane fuel cell.
  • Then we talk about oxygen sensors.
  • And then supercapacitors and finally Ragoni plot.
  • Battery is a device which stores chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy on demand.
  • We said that they are devices which convert chemical energy stored in the reaction into electrical energy.
  • Another property of battery is that they come in variables, shapes, and sizes.
  • You can have batteries which are very tiny like the ones which are used in hearing aids, or you can have batteries which are very huge like.
  • They could weigh up to 200 tons and they are used in submarines.
  • And also the shapes of the batteries can be varied depending on the application.
  • And the third most important point about batteries is that they are portable.
  • You can carry them into space, you can use them on the land, and you can also take them underwater.
  • Three important properties of batteries which make them very useful.
  • We all know that there are a lot of applications of for batteries like in consumer goods.
  • We have mobiles, laptops, calculators, flashlights on one hand.
  • And on the other hand, we have very specific applications like in emergency lighting.
  • space vehicles, electric vehicles, and pacemakers.
  • We know that a battery is a galvanic cell, therefore we will require the two electrodes, anode and cathode.
  • What material would I choose for the anode?
  • It has to be something which undergoes oxidation very easily.
  • Therefore, we find most of the batteries they use metals as the electroactive material at anode.
  • And most commonly used materials for batteries are zinc, lead and lithium.
  • Most of the batteries now are being made with lithium.
  • And we also need a cathode where reduction takes place.
  • We know that oxidation and reduction should happen simultaneously.
  • And please remember this that a metal can never undergo reduction.
  • It can undergo oxidation.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let us look at the various components of a battery.

These are edited study notes based on the cited lecture interval. Check uncertain speech recognition against the source transcript and recording.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

But it can never undergo reduction for the simple reason that it's already in the lowest reduced form.

Key details

  • Metal in the form of iron.
  • That means in the form of compounds.
  • Metal itself is used as the anode, but at the cathode we use compounds of metals which can undergo reduction easily.
  • Then MnO2 is also an oxide which is used.
  • Not only oxides, we can use chlorides, nitrates, any of the compounds, but most commonly used are oxides.
  • And we can even use oxygen as the cathode active material because we know that oxy can undergo reduction easily.
  • What would serve as an electrolyte?
  • Substances which have very good ionic conductivity.
  • Ionic conductivity means we need ions which will move very easily from one electrode to the other.
  • We can have acids, we can have alkali, we can have salt solutions, we can also have molten salts.
  • And also because molten salt can produce ions which are free to move.
  • And we can also have solids which are doped oxides.
  • And then we can have polymers also which can be used as electrolytes.
  • NAFion is a polymer membrane which is used in some batteries.
  • Then we come to the last component that is a separator.
  • What is a separator?
  • It's usually an insulator which is going to separate the anode and the cathode compartment.
  • It is to prevent the anode and cathode coming in contact with each other because if that happens, there's going to be internal short circuit.
  • To separate the anode and the cathode.
  • But at the same time, it should be able to transport the ions because apart from the oxidation and reduction which is happening at the anode and cathode, respectively, this transport of ions in the through the electrolyte is very important for the battery to function.
  • Therefore the electro the separator should be able to transport the ions from anode to cathode and cathode to anode.
  • There are many types of separators which are employed based on the design of the battery.
  • But this anode active material may be in the form of a powder or a paste and therefore we need what we call as a current collector.
  • Always there will be a current collector.
  • The current collector itself is not involved in the reaction.
  • It is the it is the electroactive species which is involved in the reaction.
  • And then on the cathode health also we have a similar.
  • Electroactive species, but this is the cathode electroactive species, and this will be the current collector.
  • active material and here we have the anode active material.
  • Then what do we need next?
  • We use the anode material, we use the cathode material, and then we need the electrolyte.
  • It is present between the anode and cathode and it is going to make sure the anode and cathode do not come in contact.

Example or application from the lecture

  • And most of the times we find lead oxide is a good example, like in your lead acid battery.
  • So for example, we can have H2SO4, we can use H2SO4 or KOH or Nafion.

Core explanation · 10:00–14:59

Okay and then we also have terminals here, which you are aware because we all use a lot of batteries.

Key details

  • we have placed inside the battery.
  • So inner battery, therefore, so both are terminals here.
  • And this whole thing is now kept inside a housing it is called it's a container into which this anode and cathode reactive materials along with the current collectors are placed and this is filled with electrolyte and there's a separator separating the anode and the cathode.
  • Now the battery can discharge because we know it is going it is a source of energy, it is source of power.
  • What do you mean by discharge?
  • It is delivering power.
  • When the battery discharges, we it is delivering power.
  • So therefore it acts like a galvanic cell.
  • Again, galvanic cell uses the chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy.
  • Therefore, when the battery is discharging and giving us power, the battery.
  • Bacteria is behaving like a galvanic cell.
  • They move through the external wire and at the cathode we have some species say A, which is going to take up these n electrons, and we get A N minus.

  • Certain interstitial hydrides are very suitable for hydrogen storage and transportation

  • hydrogen can be released whenever required by thermal stimulation or any other technique
  • Cooling and compression process consume energy (net loss about 30%)

Principle Features and Content e) 1. Prevent Waste The primary goal is to synthesize the target product with little to no by- products or waste. Waste treatment adds to costs. 2. Atom Economy Maximize the incorporation of reactants into the final product. Aim for 100% atom economy using addition/rearrangement reactions. 3. Safer Synthesis Minimize or avoid hazardous substances in synthesis. Example: Use CO, instead of toxic phosgene in polyurethane synthesis. 4. Safe Products Products should be effective but with reduced toxicity. Minimize harmful side effects on users and the environment. 5. Design Benign Chemicals Use safer solvents/reaction conditions. Avoid harmful solvents like chloroform; prefer water, CO,, ionic liquids, or solvent-free systems. 6. Design for Energy Efficiency Reduce energy intensity by using catalysts (e.g., bio-catalysts) and modern methods like microwave or ultrasound irradiation. 7. Use of Renewable Feedstock Prefer renewable raw materials like biomass over non-renewable sources such as coal and petroleum. 8. Reduce Derivatives Avoid unnecessary derivatization steps (e.g., blocking/protecting groups) to minimize waste and enhance atom efficiency. 9. Catalysis Use catalysts to accelerate reactions, reduce energy use, and achieve high yields with recyclable, selective reactions. 10. Design for Degradation Products should degrade into harmless substances after use to prevent environmental accumulation (e.g., pesticides, polymers). 11. Pollution Prevention Employ real-time monitoring and control of processes to prevent hazardous substances. Recycle unreacted chemicals. 12. Accident Prevention Choose chemicals and processes to minimize risks of accidents like fires, explosions, and toxic releases. Equip facilities with safety measures.

notes.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

We will continue with module two on nanomaterials and in this class we are going to talk about properties of nanomaterials, surface area dependent properties, electrical properties and optical properties.

Key details

  • Properties of nanomaterials are very different from that of the bulk materials.
  • We find that for bulk material the properties are independent of size whereas when we come to nanomaterials they change with size.
  • Then it is it has a particular colour that is called golden colour.
  • There is no change in the colour, it still continues to remain in that golden colour.
  • But that is not true when we come to the nanoparticle range.
  • Gold, when we get it into the nanoparticle range, we find that as we decrease the size, the colour of gold also.
  • That the optical properties are getting altered with the dimension of the particles.
  • Is what happens for all most of the properties of nanomaterials.
  • They change with size.
  • Whereas in nanomaterials, the material remains the same.
  • The structure composition remains the same, it's only the size which is changing, and that can alter the properties.
  • We know that many physical and chemical properties of a material are going to depend on surface properties, and when we come to nanomaterials, the surface area has enormously increased.
  • We have a bulk material over here, it is being broken down into smaller particles.
  • We know that the surface area has increased so much over here.
  • The surface area.
  • And we know that since in nanomaterials the surface atoms are much more than what the atoms at inside the bulk of the material and therefore.
  • All the properties are mostly dictated by the surface atoms.
  • And since we have such a large surface area, such a large number of surface atoms, therefore the properties which depend on surface area definitely get affected when you take.
  • the particle when take the material from bulk to nanocyte.
  • So properties like catalytic activity we know that whenever we use a catalyst we prefer to take it in the powder form because we want to increase the surface area and catalytic catalysis is a surface phenomena.
  • If we take it in nano range, nano particle range, the catalytic activity is going to increase enormously.
  • Are found to be catalytically very active for selective redox reactions.
  • Because there are a lot of surface atoms which are held much less tightly as compared to the bulk atoms.
  • For nanoparticles, it is found that electrical conductivity decreases as compared to the bulk material.
  • One important reason for that is spatial confinement.
  • We talked about spatial confinement also, and we understood that as we go into the nanoparticle range.

Example or application from the lecture

  • For example, if we have a block of gold.
  • Now even if you make it into smaller and smaller size, like for example, the block of gold which was say hundred grams, now we make it into a five gram piece, by breaking it into smaller pieces, we find that.
  • Let us look at the most important property of nanomaterials, the surface area.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

The energy levels become more and more discrete, and the band gap increases or the energy gap increases.

Key details

  • What are we talking about here?
  • Now when we have metals, we know that the valence band and the conductance band are overlapping and therefore the.
  • Electrons can easily move into the conduction band and we find that metals are good conductors.
  • Whereas in insulators the energy gap is very high and therefore they are not found to conduct electricity.
  • Whereas in semiconductors the band gap is less.
  • Energy gap is less now, and therefore, it is possible that if we give the right energy, the electrical conduction is possible.
  • You can see the same energy.
  • Semiconductor now the band gap has become more and obviously when the band gap is more than the conductivance properties are going to get altered.
  • you can see here this the band gap is so high, so obviously the conductance has become less and they can almost be acting like insulators.
  • Another important reason is due to surface scattering.
  • What is a mean free part for an electron?
  • the distance which the electrons move before they undergo some collusion.
  • We know that the electron has a mean prepared and there's no obstruction.
  • But when we have the same bulk material into the nanoparticle range, now we know that the nanoparticle has become has a very small dimension.
  • Changing its direction and therefore there is conservation of energy as well as momentum.
  • Whereas if it is inelastic scattering, then when the electron is scattered in randomly in all directions.
  • We find that the scattered electron now loses its velocity, and when the electron loses its velocity, it's understood that the.
  • Mobility is now less and therefore the electrical conductivity decreases.
  • Coming to the next property that is optical properties.
  • Nanomaterials show unique optical properties.
  • As I mentioned, the colour depends on the size of the particles.
  • In the bulk material, there is no change in colour even if you decrease the size.
  • But when you come into the nano range, it is found that as we change the size of the particles, there is a change in colour.
  • One is due to the surface plasmon resonance and the other is due to increase in band gap.
  • If you look at metals.
  • This is the picture of a metal.
  • What happens is the.
  • Electric field which is fluctuating, the electromagnetic radiation which is formed falling on the surface, it has an electric field.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let's understand what is the surface plasmon resonance.

Core explanation · 10:00–14:59

Because the lattice point is positive, these is an electron cloud which is getting formed, there is an attraction which is going to pull these electrons back.

Key details

  • Up in the in the system.
  • This collective oscillation of these electrons is what is known as the plasmon.
  • Collective oscillations of these electrons is what is known as plasma.

Weak Binding Forces: Hydrogen storage materials have high specific surface areas but weak binding forces (e.g., Van der Waals forces). 2. Metal Decorations: Metal decorations are effective in increasing the bonding energy of hydrogen on sorption-based materials. 3. Hydrogen Spillover: e Hydrogen storage in carbon materials is enhanced by decorating these materials with transition metals. ¢ Definition: Hydrogen spillover refers to the migration of hydrogen atoms from the metal surface to anon-metal support or absorbent.

notes.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we are going to learn about unit one.

Key details

  • In that, topic one, an introduction to semiconductor.
  • The three semiconductors which is most commonly or most frequently used in the construction of electronic devices are germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide.
  • And we also see that the atomic structure of silicon and germanium.
  • First, if you look at the atomic structure of silicon, the atomic number is 14, and it's represented in terms of SPDF model one S two, two S two, two P six, three S two.
  • And if you start arranging with respect to the shell around, we call it as orbits.
  • So the first orbit can have two, second can have eight, and the remaining four, that is three S two, three P two are at the outside.
  • We call it as a valence shell, which has four valence electron.
  • That means to say, they are not stable.
  • But before that, they try to balance by themselves by moving from lower energy level to the higher energy level.
  • There is a no gap at all.
  • There's an overlapping in the case of a conductor between the conduction band and the valence band.
  • Whereas in the case of a semiconductor, as we see, there is a little gap compared to the insulator and conductor.
  • The term intrinsic is applied to any semiconductor material that carefully refine to reduce the number of impurities to a very low level.
  • That is, we can call it as a pure form, made available through modern technology.
  • Whereas extrinsic semiconductor are those that can be subjected to doping process with the impurities being added to that.
  • Even in the upper part, even in the lower, even in the lower and also the side we see that there is a covalent bond where valence electrons are shared.
  • With the increase in the voltage, the semiconductor act like a conductor where covalent bond is ruptured, with the temperature reduced act like an insulator where the covalent bonds are not ruptured.
  • We know the four valence electrons are shared with the neighboring silicon atom, and one is free, the fifth valence electron of the antimony is free.
  • And if you apply the voltage to this bonding arrangement, and covalent bond is ruptured, one more electrons will get free up.
  • That means the number of electrons are more compared to the holes here.

Example or application from the lecture

  • For example, if you look at the first diagram here, as marked here, where the impurity added is the antimony impurity has been added, where outermost five valence electrons are there.

notes.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we're going to learn about avalanche breakdown and Zener breakdown.

Key details

  • Before that, we'll go for refreshing of the last topic, comparison of the diode characteristics of germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide.
  • We see that there are different voltages at which the different semiconductor device has different conducting voltages and with respect to forward bias and reverse bias.
  • In the forward bias, we see the germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide, which conduct at different voltages.
  • The reverse bias also, the breakdown also occurs at different voltages.
  • The first is avalanche breakdown for a normal diode we look at.
  • The forward bias region is this, the reverse bias region is this.
  • So in the reverse bias condition, as the voltage increases, the free charge carriers obtain velocity and associated kinetic energy and release additional carriers through collision with the other atomic structure.
  • Hence, the covalent bonds are broken and electron-hole pair are generated.
  • This electron will hit to the walls of an atom, as we see here, and acquire a energy from applied voltage.
  • This will hit based on the energy acquired from applied voltage and produce more and more free electrons.
  • This free electron again will hit the another atoms, and this cumulative process is called avalanche multiplication or ionization process.
  • The Zener breakdown occurs when both P and N-type materials are heavily doped in a semiconductor diode, hence depletion region is narrowed down, as we see from the diagram here.
  • When a small reverse voltage is applied across the diode, a very strong electric field is produced.
  • Due to this electric field, covalent bonds breaks and produce a large number of free charge carriers.
  • So coming to the comparison between the Zener breakdown and avalanche breakdown, first we start with Zener, and on the right-hand side we have avalanche.
  • The first point is, the process in which the electron move across a barrier from valence band of the p-type material to the conduction band of n-type material is known as breakdown voltage, whereas the process of applying a high voltage and increasing the free electron.
  • Coming to the second point, this is observed in a.
  • Zener diode having a Zener breakdown, which varies from five to eight volts, whereas in the case of an avalanche breakdown, this is observed in the normal diode having a voltage greater than the eight volts.
  • Number three, the valence electrons are pulled out into a conduction due to the high electric field in the narrow depletion region.
  • Here, the valence electrons are pushed to the conduction due to the energy imparted with the accelerated electron which gain their velocity due to the collision with other atom.
  • Coming to the fourth point, the increase in temperature decreases with the breakdown voltage.
  • The increase in temperature will increase the breakdown voltage here.
  • The VI characteristics of Zener diode breakdown has sharp value.
  • The VI characteristics of avalanche breakdown is not sharp as.
  • Zener breakdown, as we see from the diagram.
  • Then in the Zener, it occurs in diode that are lightly doped.
  • The effect of variation in the temperature across the semiconductor diode is observed in both forward as well as the reverse characteristics.
  • The rise in temperature generates more electron-hole pair, thus conductivity increases and thus increase in the current.
  • The PN junction diode parameter like reverse saturation current, bias current, reverse breakdown voltage, and barrier voltage are dependent on the temperature.
  • Increase in temperature increases the carrier concentration.
  • As a result, the knee voltage decreases, breakdown voltage increases, while the reverse saturation current also increases.
  • This we can understand with the help of a forward bias and a reverse.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let us also consider the effect of temperature on VI characteristics of the diode.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

Under reverse bias, the change in the temperature across the diode, the reverse saturation current of the diode increases with increase in temperature.

Key details

Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

In this session, we will small problems on Lagrange Method.

Key details

  • Find the dimensions of the rectangle box open at the top of maximum capacity whose surface is 432 square centimeter.

  • Because we need to find out the dimensions that is XYZ of this rectangular box.
  • This volume xyz becomes function for the problem and xy plus 2yz plus 2 z equals 432 becomes constraint for the problem.
  • plus 2 zx minus 432 equals 0.
  • That is xy plus two yz plus two zx minus four thirty two.
  • Next, as per the procedure, we need to compute the partial derivative of f with respect to x, y, as well as z.
  • Then we equate fx to zero.
  • That leads to yz lambda of y plus two z equals zero.
  • of f with respect to y equals zero gives x plus lambda x plus two z equals zero.
  • We see that 2z lambda of x minus y equals 0.
  • Because 2z lambda is not zero, we can equate x minus y equals 0, then that gives x equals y.
  • Similarly, multiply 2 by y and 3 by z and subtracting we get x lambda of y minus 2 z t equals 0 because x lambda not zero we can equate y minus 2 z to 0 that gives y equal to 2 z.
  • Substitute x equals y, y equals to z in the constant and for you have x y z.
  • We see that.
  • 3x square equals 432 or x equals 12.

  • Because z is y by 2, z becomes 6.
  • So this is how we can solve problem using Lagrange method.

Let's look at the second problem.

Key details

  • Divide the number 24 into three parts such that the continued product of the first square of the second and the cube of the third may be maximum.
  • Continued product means the product we get by multiplying together in succession.
  • Then divide the number 24 into three parts.
  • It means we want to split 24 into three non-negative parts.
  • X plus Y plus Z minus 24.
  • F to zero gives two x y z power three plus lambda zero.
  • Observe carefully in all these three expressions, we can use this idea.

  • Differential equations are classified into two based on the number of independent variables present in it.
  • The first one ordinary differential equations and partial differential equations.
  • In the case of ordinary differential equations, we see that the derivatives are with respect to only one independent variable.
  • Also, the unknown function depends on a single variable.
  • And X is independent variable.
  • In a similar way, in partial differential equations we see that the partial derivatives are with respect to two or more independent variables.
  • The unknown function depends on multiple variables.
  • In this case u is dependent variable and x and t are independent variables.
  • A partial differential equation is an equation that involves partial derivatives of a function with several independent variables.
  • As in the case of ordinary differential equations, we have only one independent variable.
  • In the case of partial differential equations, we have two or more independent variables.

notes.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

I'm Sibashankari from the Department of Science and Humanities.

Key details

  • For the semester, in the lab session, we will cover basics of MATLAB, programming in MATLAB, plotting 2D and 3D, and then linear algebra, partial differentiation, and solving differential equation.
  • And the reference books are "Getting Started with MATLAB" by Rudra Pratap, and the "MATLAB for Engineers" by Holly Moore, and then "MATLAB Programming for Engineers" by Stephen J.
  • The whole syllabus will be covered in 12 sessions, and this is the first session in MATLAB.
  • Hope everyone would have downloaded the MATLAB software.
  • In case if you have not downloaded, then you can use the installation guidelines link that is attached along with this video.
  • As that MATLAB is a paid software, and so if you have institution mail.
  • ID, then you can get the access to licensed version.
  • Otherwise, you need to download the trial version.
  • MATLAB is a software package for numerical computation, visualization, and programming.
  • It provides an interactive environment with hundreds of built-in function for technical computation, graphics, and animation.
  • The name MATLAB stands for Matrix Laboratory because the basic building block of MATLAB is the matrix.
  • Some basic features and commands of MATLAB.
  • It consists of MATLAB desktop, a figure window, and an editor window.
  • The figure window opens automatically when graphic commands are executed and contains graph created by these command.
  • The editor window is used for writing and editing programs.
  • This is the place where you can write, edit, create, or save your own program in files called M files.
  • We can see the MATLAB desktop, which contains three sub-windows, command window, current folder, and the workspace.
  • This is the default layout.
  • If you want to change the layout, click on the layout option here and change as per your preference.
  • Other two windows are not displayed.
  • This is the main window where we write the commands as well as see the outputs.
  • In other words, here is the interaction with the software.
  • So to type a command, the cursor must be placed next to the command prompt.
  • To start with, we can use this command window as a calculator where you can type in commands line by line.

Example or application from the lecture

  • To begin with, let us look at the general structure of MATLAB environment.
  • Suppose if I select the three column, then the current folder, command window, and the workspace appear in column-wise.
  • Suppose if I select it as command window only, then you could see only the command window.

These are edited study notes based on the cited lecture interval. Check uncertain speech recognition against the source transcript and recording.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

Once a command is typed, to execute the command, Enter key is pressed.

Key details

  • Whenever a calculation is performed, MATLAB will assign the result to the built-in variable ans, unless specified.
  • That is the answer variable.
  • And ans is the default output variable.
  • The easy way to do is, is to use an assignment operator.
  • Use the assignment operator, which is equal sign, and then any value or mathematical expression we can give.
  • And you should remember that, or make a note of it, the variable must be always on the left, and the expression or the value should be on the right.
  • Otherwise, an error will occur if they are reversed.
  • And one more thing is that if I type b plus four equal to 66, see, this is an incorrect assignment statement.
  • It takes small a and capital A as two different variable.
  • That is, the variable should not start with a number.
  • It should always start with the alphabet.
  • I cannot assign it this way.
  • Instead, if I assign a4 equal to 20, it will accept.
  • It should start with alphabet.
  • And we should avoid using the names of built-in function for variable.
  • As my variable, sin equal to 66, then sin variable is created and the value 66 is stored in that sin variable.

Example or application from the lecture

Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

My name is Dr.

Key details

  • SV Venkatish from Civil Engineering and the Department of Science and Humanities PS University.
  • Two chapters which are there in unit one, chapter one and chapter two.
  • In chapter one, we had discussed a few of the definitions and the units of forces.
  • In chapter two, we had four topics.
  • One as resolution of forces.
  • In that you have rectangular components, N and T components, then axes which are not at 90 degrees, then the difference between projection and components.
  • That's topic one under chapter two.
  • The second topic was on movement.
  • We discussed moment, varingance principle, and we have solved problems on moment also.
  • That's second topic.
  • The third topic was on couple.
  • We have seen what is the definition of couple, characteristics of couple, classification of couple, effects of couple, and very importantly, what do you mean by force couple system?
  • And then we have solved problems on that.
  • The last topic in unit one, chapter two, is resulted.
  • We have discussed what is resulted, how do we determine the characteristics of resultant, four characteristics that is magnitude, direction, sense, and point of application.
  • To determine the point of application, we have used principle of moments, okay, and then we have solved problems on that.
  • To certain extent unit 3 also.
  • You have the background of unit one.
  • We will now get into unit two.
  • And the prescribed textbook that we are using is engineering mechanics statics.
  • Very importantly, it is the eighth edition, which is in SI version.
  • And the author is Miriam Craig and adopted by Bolton.
  • There's one more in this other than equilibrium, we also have trusses.
  • We will discuss that later when we take up that topic.
  • So first we will discuss about chapter three, which is equilibrium.
  • What is equilibrium?
  • If the resultant force and the resultant movement acting on a body on which there are several.
  • Forces and moments acting, that is a system of forces are acting.
  • If the resultant force and moment both of them are zero, then we say that the body is in equilibrium.
  • Application of the force would be a rotatory motion which will make this body to rotate.
  • It won't move.
  • But you can also have a combination of transmitter motion as well as rotatory motion.
  • It ensures that there is no transmitter emotion.
  • Why I'm saying this?
  • Because as you could see, the net force because of a couple is zero.
  • But what is the effect of a couple?
  • It makes the body to rotate.
  • It should not get displaced, it should not rotate also.
  • But if we take this, m is equal to 0, or algebraic sum of all the moments of all the forces at any point, at any point should be equal to 0.
  • This will ensure that there is no rotatory motion.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

Ensure or to show that the body is in equilibrium or to determine the forces which makes the body to be in equilibrium.

Key details

  • What is that?
  • The first thing is a free body diagram.
  • We have already discussed about free body diagram.
  • But since it comes exclusively in this chapter, I am again arbitrating or bringing the concept of a free body diagram.
  • As the name suggests, free body diagram is a diagram in which we will have a diagram.
  • Such that there is no body in that.
  • The diagram will have the forces, the characteristics of forces which are acting on the body, and we were going to remove that body because we are not interested in the body.
  • What we are interested is what are the forces that is acting on the body, what is the effect of that.
  • That is what is called as a free body diagram, as I suggest, as the name itself suggests, we are making the diagram free of the body.
  • Position means the point of application.
  • In the solution of problems in mechanics, if how to draw the free body diagram, fifty percent of the problem is solved when it comes to equilibrium chapter.
  • But that free body diagram should be clear and sufficient for you to determine the unknowns.
  • A few of these supports we have already discussed in our unit one.
  • The first type of support is a flexible cable or belt or chain or rope.
  • It is a body which can support tensile forces.
  • When I say tensile forces, if you have a rope and if you try to pull it, okay, once it is tight, afterwards it will not move.
  • For this type of support where you have a flexible cable or a bolt, or sorry, belt, or a chain, or a rope.
  • It can resist tensile forces, and that is what is indicated here.
  • So this, if I try to pull this it will not move because of this oh.
  • And there's a tension here, the internal forces will be acting towards each other and that is what is indicated here.
  • If I cut it here and look at this, I will get the force to be this.
  • There will be only one force with no line of action.
  • If you are looking at what is the force acting on the in the row, then it is internal.
  • If you are looking at what is the force causing the tension is the external force.
  • The second one is a smooth surface.
  • A smooth surface is one in which you will have one reaction with known line of action.
  • Which will always act perpendicular to the surface.
  • This is the surface.
  • And this is the reaction that we get and this angle is always ninety degrees and the sense is going to be opposite to the body weight that is acting.
  • The body weight will be acting here, so you will have the normal reaction acting here.
  • There won't be any friction when it comes to smooth surface.
  • Or the frictional force that develops because of the smooth surface would be quite less when compared to the force that is acting.
  • The next category is a rough surface.
  • You have already studied about this.
  • If the roughness of the body which are in contact with each other is quite large.
  • Then it will prevent the body from moving tangential to the surface, and that we call it as frictional force.
  • In addition to this frictional force, we will also have a normal reaction.

Example or application from the lecture

  • You can also have a roller vertical or inclined also.

  • In this case the line of roller is horizontal in all the four cases.
  • You can also have vertical if the rollers are to the left, then you will have the support reaction acting to the right.
  • If you have the rollers.

  • The next one is a freely sliding guide.
  • In this case, you will have one reaction only.
  • In this case, you can see that the sliding guide can move horizontally, it cannot move vertically.
  • The reaction can be upwards or downwards.
  • Along the horizontal, it can move only this much.
  • After which, if it moves till here, then it cannot move.

  • That is why it is called as freely sliding train.

  • But however, here what is indicated for this position is there will be only one normal reaction, normal reacting vertically.
  • Continuing the different types of supports, the next one comes.
  • Pin connection, look at how the pin connection is indicated.
  • There is a clear difference between a pin connection and a roller connection.
  • In case of rollers, you will have roller here and then you will have a the surface.
  • Whereas pin connection, directly the triangle is resting on the surface.
  • The door frame or the door itself is fixed to the frame of the door.
  • In case of hinges, you will have two reaction.
  • No, you cannot move the door upwards or downwards.
  • Toward the frame, or you cannot pull it out of the frame, but you can rotate the door.
  • That is permitted in case of the door.
  • That is what the hint support does.
  • It will provide you two reactions.
  • It will permit you to rotate.
  • In the plane opposite to this two reaction that is coming.
  • If this is X and Y, it will rotate along the Z axis.
  • No, you have a door with a stopper.
  • Doe stopper, we are we know the door stopper.

  • That is why you can see here.

  • The next one is a fixed or a built-end support.
  • This is welded connection, this is fixed.
  • The sense of this, even here the sense of this reactions can be upwards or downwards, right side or left side, clockwise or anti-clockwise based on the force that is acting on the body.
  • Then we have also looked at gravitational force earlier.
  • Always the gravitational force will be acting downwards.

Example or application from the lecture
